The Federal Government says it has restored electricity supply to several areas in Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Kwara and the Federal Capital Territory following disruptions caused partly by the vandalism of a critical 330-kilovolt transmission line. The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this in an update posted on social media on Monday, saying the affected Benin-Egbin transmission line had been repaired and returned to service. The restoration has increased electricity supply to the Lagos Complex to more than 1,000 megawatts, bringing the system back to the level recorded before the disruption. The development comes amid renewed concerns over the vulnerability of Nigeria’s electricity transmission infrastructure and the recurring interruptions that have left homes, businesses and public institutions without reliable power. The minister said, “I would like to report that power has since been restored to many of the areas earlier affected by power disruptions, largely in Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Kwara and the FCT. Our teams continue to work to restore full supply to the remaining affected locations. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. This restoration helped to bring the total power supply to the Lagos Complex to over 1,000 megawatts, effectively normalising to the condition before the disruption.” He added that the ministry was working with generation companies, the system operator, the Transmission Company of Nigeria and electricity distribution companies to prevent further deterioration in supply. The latest update follows an earlier explanation by Tegbe that planned maintenance at Egbin Power Station, inadequate gas supply to some thermal power plants and damage to critical transmission infrastructure had combined to reduce electricity available on the national grid. Lagos pledges start-up support for 203 youths Lagos monarch appeals court order nullifying his installation Power outages: DisCos apologise to Nigerians In his earlier statement last Friday, the minister had acknowledged the hardship caused by the outages, particularly for households and businesses in Lagos and the FCT. “Planned maintenance at Egbin Power Station and constraints in gas supply to some thermal power stations have reduced the amount of electricity available on the national grid. Grid operators have, therefore, implemented load shedding in some areas to manage the shortfall,” he said. Tegbe had also disclosed that sabotage of key transmission lines restricted the use of alternative routes for delivering electricity, particularly to Lagos. The minister had promised that affected generating units would return to service in phases, with the first units expected to resume operation within 48 to 72 hours. The restoration of the Benin-Egbin line is significant because the Lagos electricity network depends on multiple transmission routes to receive bulk power from generating stations. Damage to one route can reduce the amount of electricity available to the Lagos transmission complex, particularly when other sources of supply are constrained. The minister further disclosed on Monday that the government was working to restore another important transmission route, the Osogbo-Ikeja West 330kV line, which has remained out of service for about 18 months. Speaking on a television programme, Tegbe said the line could deliver an additional 400MW to Lagos but had been affected by the vandalism of about six transmission towers located in a swampy area. He said the government had secured a commitment from the TCN to complete the restoration by the end of November.
